title: Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning - Cooperative Procurement
subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Which of the following is the best definition of cooperative procurement?
options: An agency dividing a single large contract into smaller awards among multiple vendors.
Two or more public procurement entities combining their requirements to obtain volume pricing and administrative efficiency.
The process of a buyer negotiating directly with a sole source vendor.
When private corporations join together to supply a government entity.
questions.explain: Cooperative procurement involves two or more entities combining their requirements to leverage volume and share administrative efforts, typically executed via lead-agency or national cooperative contracts.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: When one entity conducts the competitive solicitation and awards a contract that includes a clause allowing other eligible public entities to use the contract, this is known as:
options: Joint solicitation.
Piggybacking.
Spot purchasing.
Maverick buying.
questions.explain: Piggybacking occurs when one agency 'rides' a contract competitively established by another agency, provided the original contract contains language (a piggyback clause) permitting extended use.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Before utilizing a national cooperative contract for a major software acquisition, the public buyer must FIRST verify:
options: That the cooperative contract was awarded to a vendor located in their own state.
That the cooperative pays administrative fees back to the buying agency.
That the lead agency's competitive process complied with the using agency's local and state procurement statutes.
That the software requires absolutely no customization.
questions.explain: A fundamental rule of cooperative purchasing is 'due diligence'. The using agency must ensure the lead agency's solicitation process meets the legal and statutory requirements of the using agency's jurisdiction.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A 'Joint Solicitation' cooperative method is distinct from 'Piggybacking' because in a joint solicitation:
options: Two or more agencies combine their known quantities into a single initial bid to maximize immediate leverage, rather than one agency buying off an existing contract.
It can only be used between federal and state governments.
No contract is formally awarded; it acts only as an RFI.
The vendor signs separate terms and conditions with every single taxpayer in the district.
questions.explain: In a joint solicitation, participating agencies pool their definite volume upfront in the initial IFB/RFP. Piggybacking is an after-the-fact usage of an already awarded contract where initial volume wasn't specifically pooled.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: What is the role of a 'Lead Agency' in a national cooperative purchasing program?
options: It legally indemnifies all other agencies from any breach of contract by the vendor.
It dictates what budget other entities can allocate.
It is the government entity that officially issues the solicitation, conducts the evaluation, and awards the master agreement.
It manufactures the goods being procured.
questions.explain: The lead agency acts as the contracting authority. It handles the competitive procurement process on behalf of itself and the broader cooperative membership, legally establishing the master contract.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A buyer is defending the use of a national cooperative contract to local businesses who complain they did not see the bid advertised locally. What is the most accurate justification?
options: Cooperative contracts are exempt from fair and open competition principles.
The cooperative contract was formally competed on a national level by the lead agency, providing volume discounts that represent best value for local taxpayers.
Local businesses are not permitted to bid on national contracts.
The buyer prefers not to evaluate local vendor submissions.
questions.explain: Cooperative contracts fulfill the requirement for competition (handled by the lead agency). Buyers justify their use because the pooled national volume typically yields a lower administrative burden and better pricing, serving the taxpayers' best financial interest.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: State and local governments are often permitted to use specific Federal General Services Administration (GSA) schedules. For example, GSA Schedule 70 is primarily utilized for:
options: Heavy construction and infrastructure materials.
Information Technology (IT) equipment, software, and services.
Disaster relief medical supplies.
Local landscaping services.
questions.explain: Under the GSA Cooperative Purchasing Program, state and local governments can purchase IT products and services from GSA Multiple Award Schedule (MAS) 70 (now part of the consolidated MAS under the IT category).
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: In many cooperative purchasing agreements, the vendor pays an 'administrative fee' (e.g., 1-2% of sales) back to the cooperative organization. What is the primary purpose of this fee?
options: To provide a kickback to the individual buyers.
To fund the administrative operations of the cooperative organization that managed and maintains the contract.
To penalize the vendor for using a cooperative contract.
To pay the freight and shipping costs for all using agencies.
questions.explain: The administrative fee covers the operational costs of the cooperative program or lead agency that bears the expense of soliciting, managing, and marketing the master contract.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A city buyer finds a piggybackable contract from a neighboring county for patrol vehicles. The city requires specialized sirens not listed on the county's contract. How should the buyer proceed?
options: Add the specialized sirens to the PO under the cooperative contract anyway, as they are minor accessories.
Piggyback the vehicles and issue a separate, compliant procurement for the specialized sirens and installation.
Cancel the idea of using the cooperative completely.
Require the neighboring county to rebid the entire contract to include the sirens.
questions.explain: A user agency cannot add items to a cooperative contract that were not competitively priced or included in the original award (scope creep). Purchasing off-contract items violates competition rules. They must be procured separately.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: When assessing a cooperative contract for use, a public buyer conducts a price analysis. They find the cooperative's prices for copy paper are 15% higher than what they previously paid to a local vendor. The buyer should:
options: Use the cooperative anyway because it is easier.
Decline to use the cooperative contract, as it does not represent the best value based on current market conditions.
Report the cooperative to the federal government for price gouging.
Require the local vendor to match the higher cooperative price.
questions.explain: Cooperative contracts are a tool, not a mandate. If local or independent market analysis shows the agency can obtain better value independently, the agency should not use the cooperative contract.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: NASPO ValuePoint is an example of:
options: A federal law mandating open bidding.
A national cooperative purchasing program primarily facilitating state-led public contracts.
A reverse auction software platform.
A bonding surety company.
questions.explain: NASPO ValuePoint is a prominent national cooperative purchasing program established by the National Association of State Procurement Officials. It facilitates multi-state public cooperative contracts.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: To legally use another agency's contract via piggybacking, the using agency must execute which of the following documents to establish privity of contract and attach their local legal terms?
options: A Participating Addendum (PA) or Interlocal Agreement.
A Notice to Proceed.
An Invitation to Bid.
A Sole Source Justification.
questions.explain: A Participating Addendum (PA) or Interlocal Agreement is the legal mechanism that binds the using agency and the vendor, bridging the gap from the master agreement and injecting the using agency's specific statutory requirements.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: An agency requires extensive architectural and engineering (A&E) services. Can they easily utilize a national cooperative contract for this requirement?
options: Yes, A&E is treated like any standard commodity.

No, because federal/state laws (e.g., Brooks Act) generally require qualifications-based selection (QBS) uniquely tailored to local licensure and specific project requirements, making A&E highly unsuitable for national piggybacking.
Yes, but only if they pay a double administrative fee.
No, because architects are prohibited from joining cooperative networks.
questions.explain: Professional A&E services typically require a Qualifications-Based Selection process (under the Brooks Act or state equivalents) tailored to local site conditions and state licensing, making them largely ineligible or inappropriate for broad cooperative piggybacking.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: Are buyers allowed to negotiate pricing downward when using an established cooperative contract?
options: No, cooperative contract prices are legally fixed and cannot be changed.
No, attempting to negotiate voids the master agreement.
Yes, cooperative contract pricing generally establishes a ceiling; buyers are encouraged to negotiate further discounts based on specific volume or local commitments.
Yes, but only if they negotiate the price upward to support local businesses.
questions.explain: Cooperative contracts establish the maximum (ceiling) price based on the master agreement. Agencies can and should negotiate further price reductions, especially if their specific volume is substantial.
questions.subject: CPPB Domain II: Pre-Solicitation Planning

questions.q: A potential downside of an agency heavily relying on cooperative contracts for routine purchases instead of establishing their own is:
options: Faster acquisition times.
Lower administrative costs.
A loss of opportunity to develop local supplier capacity and integrate specific local socioeconomic goals into the contracts.
Automatic compliance with federal transit administration rules.
questions.explain: While efficient, national cooperative contracts often favor large, national vendors. Over-reliance can bypass local businesses and ignore specific regional socio-economic policy goals (like local MWBE programs).
